paragraphs: Kernel support vector machines can become expensive to train when datasets contain hundreds of thousands or millions of examples. This paper introduces DC-SVM, a solver that divides the training problem into smaller pieces using clustering. Each piece can be solved independently, producing local solutions that help prepare the full optimization problem.

The connection between local and global solutions is central to the approach. The analysis shows that support vectors found within the smaller problems are likely to remain support vectors for the full problem when kernel clustering partitions the data appropriately. DC-SVM then uses these local solutions to initialize a global coordinate descent solver, with the analysis supporting rapid convergence.

The authors extend this design into a multilevel method with adaptive clustering and an early prediction option. On the reported covtype experiment, it reaches the exact solution within the stated tolerance seven times faster than LIBSVM. Early prediction achieves about 96% accuracy in 12 minutes, demonstrating a practical tradeoff between finishing optimization and obtaining useful predictions sooner.
icml-2014-a-divide-and-conquer-solver-fo.tldr: DC-SVM uses clustered subproblems to accelerate kernel SVM training and provide useful predictions before global optimization finishes.

paragraphs: Topic models describe documents through mixtures of underlying topics. This paper introduces an admixture of Poisson Markov Random Fields, called APM, that can represent dependencies between words. The motivation is to make relationships among words part of the model, extending beyond the independent topic models identified in the abstract.

The authors develop a broader class of admixture models that generalizes earlier approaches. They also establish an equivalence between LDA's conditional distribution and independent Poisson distributions. This connection suggests that APM subsumes LDA's modeling power: the proposed framework has a mathematical link to an established topic model while allowing word dependencies to enter the representation.

To make parameter estimation tractable, the paper uses a pseudo log-likelihood objective. This provides a concrete estimation method alongside the more expressive model. Preliminary qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate benefits over previous models. These results support the usefulness of modeling word relationships, while their explicitly preliminary status keeps the empirical conclusion narrower than a general claim of superiority across document collections.
icml-2014-admixture-of-poisson-mrfs-a-to.tldr: APM extends topic modeling to capture word dependencies, with tractable estimation and preliminary evidence of benefits over earlier models.

paragraphs: Choosing a predictor from validation results involves uncertainty: measured performance does not identify the best candidate with certainty. This paper uses that uncertainty to construct an ensemble. Starting from a finite set of predictors, it places a prior on their performance and updates it using estimates from held-out data.

The resulting Bayesian posterior expresses uncertainty about which predictor is best. The method uses that posterior to form a weighted ensemble. Because the Bayesian reasoning concerns performance, the candidate predictors need not produce probabilities themselves. The approach also accommodates arbitrary performance measures and does not assume that any candidate generated the observed data.

The authors additionally address performance estimates obtained through k-fold cross-validation, connecting the approach to a common evaluation procedure. Their experiments report state-of-the-art performance against baselines including cross-validation-based model selection and linear combinations of predictor outputs. The contribution is a flexible way to turn evidence about predictive quality into ensemble weights, while explicitly retaining uncertainty about the choice of the best predictor.
icml-2014-agnostic-bayesian-learning-of-.tldr: Agnostic Bayesian learning builds ensembles by modeling uncertainty about candidate predictors' generalization performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify changes in time series whose observations may have arbitrary long-range dependencies. The generating distributions are unknown stationary ergodic processes, a broad setting that permits substantial dependence over time. In this framework, consistently estimating the number of change points is provably impossible without additional information.

The authors overcome that obstacle by supplying the algorithm with the correct number of distinct process distributions generating the data. This is different from supplying the number of changes: the same distribution can be relevant to multiple portions of a sequence. The extra information constrains how many underlying sources must be distinguished while leaving the changes themselves to be discovered.

Under this formulation, the paper reduces change point estimation to time series clustering. Its algorithm both counts the changes and estimates their locations, with a proof of asymptotic consistency. Empirical evaluations complement the theory. The result shows how a specific piece of prior information can make reliable estimation possible in a dependence setting where the original problem cannot be solved consistently.
icml-2014-asymptotically-consistent-esti.tldr: Knowing the number of generating process distributions enables consistent change point estimation for highly dependent time series.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs a low-rank matrix from a subset of its entries. This paper studies how the choice of observed entries affects recovery by nuclear norm minimization. Earlier guarantees based on uniformly sampled entries require strong incoherence conditions, which restrict how concentrated the matrix's structure can be.

The main result replaces those matrix restrictions with a suitable sampling rule. For an arbitrary n-by-n rank-r matrix, recovery is possible from O(nr log²(n)) entries when sampling probabilities are proportional to local row and column coherences. These quantities are closely related to leverage scores. The bound is optimal in order up to logarithmic factors, connecting recovery efficiency to where observations are collected.

Because the required coherence structure may not be known beforehand, the authors propose a two-phase sampling procedure. Numerical evidence indicates that it can perform nearly as well as sampling with that knowledge. They also quantify benefits of weighted nuclear norm minimization for an arbitrary observed set, showing how recovery can benefit from accounting for the distribution of available entries.
icml-2014-coherent-matrix-completion-cb1.tldr: Sampling according to local matrix coherence enables strong recovery guarantees without the usual incoherence restrictions.

paragraphs: Learning an orthogonal matrix requires maintaining a strict relationship among its entries throughout optimization. Ordinary updates can break orthogonality, and repairing the matrix can be computationally expensive. This paper develops an optimization framework that makes small changes while preserving the required structure.

The updates use Givens rotations, fast operations affecting a limited portion of the learned matrix. The authors present these rotations as an analogue of coordinate descent for orthogonal matrices: optimization proceeds through restricted updates that remain valid by construction. This matters because maintaining the constraint becomes part of each update rather than a separate correction after it.

The paper applies the framework to tensor decomposition for learning mixture models and to sparse principal component analysis. It also studies the parameter regime in which the Givens rotation approach converges faster and produces a superior model on a genome-wide, brain-wide mRNA expression dataset. The reported advantage is tied to that investigated regime, while the broader contribution is a reusable way to optimize orthogonal matrices.
icml-2014-coordinate-descent-for-learnin.tldr: Givens rotations provide inexpensive, orthogonality-preserving updates for learning matrices used in tensor decomposition and sparse PCA.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a deep convolutional network trained for one collection of object recognition tasks can provide useful features for substantially different visual tasks. The setting matters when the new task has too little labeled or unlabeled data to train or adapt a deep network conventionally.

The authors extract network activations and use them as fixed image representations. They compare features taken from different network levels and investigate how these features cluster images by semantic content. Their evaluation covers scene recognition, domain adaptation, and fine-grained recognition, examining transfer across several kinds of visual learning problems.

The reported results significantly outperform the existing state of the art on several evaluated vision challenges. This supports the idea that supervised training can produce representations useful beyond the original recognition tasks, including settings with limited data for adaptation. The authors also release DeCAF and the associated network parameters, making the extracted features available for further experiments with deep representations across different visual concept learning settings.
icml-2014-decaf-a-deep-convolutional-act.tldr: DeCAF shows that fixed features from a supervised convolutional network can transfer effectively to diverse visual recognition tasks.

paragraphs: Similarity search based on locality-sensitive hashing can spend much of its query time computing hashes. For high-dimensional binary data, minwise hashing commonly performs many permutations, making those evaluations costly. This paper proposes a way to generate the required hash evaluations from a single permutation.

Its central operation is a rotation scheme that densifies the sparse sketches produced by one-permutation hashing. The densification is unbiased and preserves the locality-sensitive hashing property, allowing the resulting sketches to be used for hash tables. Maintaining that property is what connects the computational shortcut to a usable similarity search method.

For an LSH configuration with K hashes per table and L tables, the stated query complexity decreases from O(dKL) to O(KL + dL), where d counts nonzero entries in the data vector. Experiments on real data report substantially shorter query processing times than minwise hashing without reduced retrieval accuracy. The authors also suggest that rotation could help densify other sparse sketches, presenting that broader application as a possibility.
icml-2014-densifying-one-permutation-has.tldr: A rotation-based densification scheme makes one-permutation hashing suitable for faster similarity search while preserving its LSH property.

paragraphs: A classifier's performance depends partly on how its examples are represented. This paper investigates scalable ways to construct features that help distinguish multiple classes, using simple second-order structure in the data. Such structure summarizes relationships between pairs of input components rather than treating each component entirely separately.

The proposed features come from generalized eigenvectors of class-conditional second moments. In plain terms, the method uses second-order summaries computed within classes to identify directions for a new representation. The approach therefore connects feature construction directly to class-specific data structure and to the needs of the downstream classification problem.

The authors establish theoretical properties of these representations, including invariance to linear transformations of the input. They also evaluate classifiers using the extracted features on three tasks and report state-of-the-art results. Together, these findings show that relatively simple statistical structure can support effective discriminative representations. The empirical success concerns the evaluated tasks, while the invariance property offers a separate mathematical reason to study the representation.
icml-2014-discriminative-features-via-ge.tldr: Generalized eigenvectors of class-specific second moments yield discriminative features with theoretical invariance properties and strong reported classification results.

paragraphs: Continuous-time Markov chains can describe systems whose possible states form enormous combinatorial spaces. Computing transition probabilities in these spaces can be difficult or infeasible. For countably infinite state spaces, the abstract identifies particle Markov chain Monte Carlo as an alternative to classical matrix-exponentiation methods.

Existing particle approaches impute both the sequence of visited states and the holding times spent in those states. This paper proposes analytically marginalizing the holding times within a particle-based Monte Carlo method. The holding times are therefore accounted for through calculation instead of being explicitly sampled along with the state sequence.

Across the tested inference settings, this change dramatically reduces the variance of the Monte Carlo approximation. With the same computational budget, the method also produces more accurate approximations to parameter posterior distributions. The experiments include synthetic and real data from string-valued mutation models in phylogenetics and nucleic acid folding pathways. These findings demonstrate the practical value of integrating out part of a complex stochastic trajectory when that calculation is available.
icml-2014-efficient-continuous-time-mark.tldr: Analytically integrating out holding times improves particle-based inference for continuous-time Markov chains in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Sparse feature selection seeks a useful predictor while limiting the number of selected features. This paper analyzes forward-backward greedy methods for smooth convex objectives. FoBa-obj requires solving many optimization problems, whereas FoBa-gdt uses gradient information to choose features during forward steps and substantially improves computational efficiency.

The authors sharpen the theoretical bounds for FoBa-obj and show that FoBa-gdt achieves the same theoretical performance under the same restricted strong convexity condition. This condition supplies the curvature needed for the analysis on restricted sets of variables. The bounds agree with those for least squares, closing a gap between that special case and more general smooth convex objectives.

The paper also gives a sufficient sample condition for restricted strong convexity: the number of independent samples exceeds the sparsity level times log d, where d is the variable dimension. In sensor selection for indoor human activity recognition, FoBa-gdt with a conditional random field objective outperforms the tested forward-greedy and L1-regularized methods. The results combine stronger guarantees with evidence for the efficient variant.
icml-2014-forward-backward-greedy-algori.tldr: Under restricted strong convexity, gradient-based FoBa matches the theoretical performance of its more computationally demanding counterpart.

paragraphs: Multi-label learning must handle examples associated with several labels, potentially drawn from an extremely large label collection. This paper addresses both the computational burden of large label spaces and the statistical challenge of incomplete label information. It frames the problem through a general empirical risk minimization objective.

Several existing label-compression methods emerge as special cases of this framework, providing a common formulation for approaches that otherwise appear separate. The authors develop efficient optimization techniques by exploiting the structure of particular losses, including squared loss. This makes the choice of objective part of the computational strategy for scaling learning.

The framework also has excess risk bounds in the presence of missing labels. The reported tight bounds favor low-rank-promoting trace-norm regularization over rank-insensitive Frobenius norm regularization in generalization performance. Benchmark experiments show substantial improvements over existing label-compression methods, and the approach scales to a Wikipedia dataset with more than 200,000 labels. These findings connect the framework's treatment of label structure to both statistical guarantees and demonstrated large-scale use.
icml-2014-large-scale-multi-label-learni.tldr: A unified risk-minimization framework supports large-scale multi-label learning with missing labels and guarantees favoring low-rank regularization.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovery of an Ising model's graph when a few nodes are connected to many others. Such hubs create a particular difficulty in high dimensions, where the number of nodes may exceed the number of independent, identically distributed samples. Existing estimators have sample requirements that grow polynomially with the largest node degree.

The authors turn the difficulty of estimating hub neighborhoods into useful information. Instead of requiring accurate estimates of these difficult components at the outset, they use quantitative indicators of the inability to estimate them. Those indicators allow the procedure to identify hub nodes even when samples are scarce.

The paper shows that this strategy supports recovery of hub-networked graphs with strong statistical guarantees in low-sample settings. The contribution is a change in how estimation difficulty is used: it becomes evidence about the graph's organization. This directly addresses the mismatch between a network containing only a few highly connected nodes and methods whose sample demands are governed by the single largest degree.
icml-2014-learning-graphs-with-a-few-hub.tldr: Quantifying difficulty in estimating neighborhoods helps identify hubs and recover hub-networked Ising graphs from few samples.

paragraphs: A document may contain many words even though only a few sentences provide the evidence needed for its category. This paper builds that intuition into the regularization used to train a text classifier. It uses sentence-level feature groupings to guide learning in a high-dimensional representation.

The method applies sparse overlapping group lasso, creating one group for the bundle of features occurring together in each training sentence. Groups can overlap because features may occur in multiple sentences. This construction connects the regularizer to the organization of the training documents, but it also creates an optimization problem containing thousands to millions of groups.

The authors show how to solve that large overlapping-group problem efficiently with the alternating direction method of multipliers. On a suite of real-world text categorization tasks, the resulting method significantly outperforms ridge, lasso, and elastic net regularization. The findings support the value of incorporating sentence-based structure into regularization and show that the resulting large collection of groups can be handled computationally.
icml-2014-making-the-most-of-bag-of-word.tldr: Sentence-based overlapping feature groups improve text categorization in the reported experiments, with ADMM making the large optimization problem tractable.

paragraphs: Some applications need the proportion of examples belonging to each class in an unlabeled collection, rather than a separate predicted label for every example. This paper studies class-ratio estimation using maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD, in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The kernel determines the representation in which distribution differences are assessed.

The authors prove that the resulting estimates are statistically consistent under stated mild conditions. They also bound estimation error using geometric quantities, including how separated the classes are and how broadly the data are spread. This makes the analysis useful for understanding which aspects of the representation affect ratio estimation.

Those theoretical insights motivate a convex formulation that automatically learns the kernel used by the estimator. An efficient cutting-plane algorithm solves that formulation. Experiments across different datasets, class proportions, and training sizes report significantly improved performance over several existing methods. The paper thus connects a conditional consistency result and interpretable error bound to a practical procedure for choosing the estimator's representation.
icml-2014-maximum-mean-discrepancy-for-c.tldr: The paper analyzes MMD-based class-ratio estimation and uses its error geometry to learn a more effective kernel.

paragraphs: Random forests are widely used, but their practical success has been harder to explain theoretically. Analyzable versions often simplify the algorithms used in applications. This paper investigates that relationship by combining a new theoretical model with empirical comparisons of simplified and practical forest methods.

The authors introduce a variant of random regression forests designed to permit mathematical analysis and prove that it is consistent. Consistency provides an asymptotic guarantee about learning as the amount of data grows. The result gives a formal foundation for the proposed variant, contributing to the understanding of forest methods.

The empirical study compares this algorithm and other theoretically tractable forest models with the random forest algorithm used in practice. Its purpose is to assess the relative importance of the simplifications introduced for analysis. These comparisons help connect mathematical tractability to observed behavior: they examine which modeling choices matter when a theoretical forest is used as a stand-in for a practical learning algorithm. The paper therefore contributes both a guarantee and evidence about the relevance of theoretical models.
icml-2014-narrowing-the-gap-random-fores.tldr: A consistent random regression forest variant and empirical comparisons clarify the relationship between tractable forest models and practical algorithms.

paragraphs: Differentially private learning seeks useful predictors while protecting information about individual training examples. This paper asks whether computationally efficient private risk minimization can avoid an explicit dependence on the number of input dimensions without requiring structural conditions such as restricted strong convexity. It gives affirmative results for particular generalized linear model settings.

For variants of output and objective perturbation, the authors establish excess risk bounds with no explicit dimension term. These results assume a convex, 1-Lipschitz loss. The bounds depend instead on the L2 norms of the true risk minimizer and training points, identifying the quantities that control the guarantee.

The paper also develops a private algorithm for optimization over the simplex with a twice-differentiable convex loss. When training points have bounded L-infinity norm, its risk bound depends only logarithmically on dimension. An online extension obtains a similarly logarithmic dimension dependence in regret, compared with the square-root dependence reported for existing private online methods. These are distinct conditional guarantees showing that ambient dimension need not enter privacy-related error bounds as strongly as before.
icml-2014-near-dimension-independent-ris.tldr: Under specified loss and norm assumptions, private generalized linear learning admits risk bounds with no explicit or only logarithmic dimension dependence.

paragraphs: Nuclear norm regularization is used in matrix optimization problems such as filling in missing matrix entries. This paper develops a solver that combines nonsmooth and smooth optimization to make these problems more efficient. Its main strategy is to select a smaller active subspace and concentrate subsequent optimization there.

At each step, a proximal gradient operation chooses the active subspace. The authors then construct a smooth, convex relaxation of the resulting smaller problem and solve it with second-order methods. The two components serve complementary purposes: one identifies a subspace to work in, while the other performs more focused optimization within that reduced setting.

On matrix completion problems including Netflix data, the methods are reported to run more than six times faster than state-of-the-art nuclear norm solvers. The paper also reports scaling such solvers to Yahoo-Music for the first time. Its comparisons show that their efficiency can compete with nonconvex methods such as alternating least squares, demonstrating that the choice of solver can substantially change the practical cost of nuclear norm optimization.
icml-2014-nuclear-norm-minimization-via-.tldr: Selecting active subspaces and solving smaller smooth problems substantially accelerates nuclear norm minimization in the reported matrix completion experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies online decision-making in finite Markov decision processes when costs change over time. It considers both full-information feedback and bandit feedback, where the learner receives more restricted observations. The authors recast the problem as online linear optimization, providing a framework for designing and analyzing learning methods.

They propose two algorithms: mirror descent with approximate projections, called MD², and continuous exponential weights with Dikin walks. The analysis combines near-optimal regret bounds with computational complexity guarantees. In particular, it includes the cost of computing approximate projections in MD², making the efficiency analysis account for an operation required to run the method.

For full-information feedback, the results complement existing work. For bandit feedback, the paper focuses on the online stochastic shortest path problem, a special case of the broader setting. There it removes a prior assumption requiring every policy to keep all state-visitation probabilities bounded away from zero. This extends the bandit result to settings that do not satisfy that restrictive visitation requirement.
icml-2014-online-learning-in-markov-deci.tldr: An online optimization formulation yields efficient MDP learning methods and removes a restrictive visitation assumption for bandit shortest-path learning.

paragraphs: This paper establishes learning guarantees for a particular class of deep generative neural networks. The networks contain n nodes, have degree at most n raised to a power γ below one, and use random edge weights in the interval [-1, 1]. These structural and randomness assumptions define the class covered by the results.

The proposed algorithm learns one layer at a time. It observes correlations among features and uses them to infer the underlying connections through a global graph recovery procedure. This connects a statistical signal in the observations to the network's hidden edge structure, providing a concrete mechanism for recovering successive layers.

The authors prove polynomial running time for learning almost all networks in this class. Depending on the model details, the required number of samples grows quadratically or cubically. The analysis also reveals structure in neural networks with random weights. The contribution is therefore a rigorous learnability result for a specified family of deep representations, with explicit computational and sample requirements tied to that family.
icml-2014-provable-bounds-for-learning-s.tldr: Layerwise correlation analysis provably learns almost all networks in a specified bounded-degree, random-weight generative class in polynomial time.

paragraphs: Randomized Fourier features approximate shift-invariant kernels, including the Gaussian kernel, so that kernel methods can train and make predictions more efficiently on large datasets. These features arise by approximating an integral with evaluations at random points. This paper investigates a different way to choose those evaluation points.

The authors replace ordinary Monte Carlo sampling with quasi-Monte Carlo sequences, which use low-discrepancy point arrangements. They derive a new measure called box discrepancy from theoretical characterizations of integration error. This supplies a criterion tailored to the approximation problem, connecting the arrangement of points to the error in the integral approximation.

The paper then proposes learning suitable quasi-Monte Carlo sequences by explicitly minimizing box discrepancy. It studies both classical sequences and sequences adapted to this setting. Empirical results support the effectiveness of these techniques alongside the theoretical analysis. The contribution is a way to improve approximate feature construction by treating the placement of integration points as a design choice, with a concrete objective for adapting those points.
icml-2014-quasi-monte-carlo-feature-maps.tldr: Quasi-Monte Carlo point sequences and a learned discrepancy criterion improve the construction of approximate Fourier kernel features.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference becomes challenging when parameters must remain inside a constrained domain. This paper proposes a Markov chain Monte Carlo framework that handles such boundaries through a geometric transformation. The aim is to generate valid sampling proposals efficiently without treating each encounter with a boundary as a separate obstacle.

The method first maps the constrained parameter domain to a unit ball, then augments that ball to a sphere. The original boundary corresponds to the sphere's equator. Movement can proceed freely on the sphere, and mapping the proposals back places them within the original constraints. The geometry therefore incorporates the boundary conditions into the sampling construction.

For computational efficiency, the authors split the dynamics into parts, one of which has an analytical solution as geodesic motion on the sphere. They evaluate the approach on truncated Gaussian distributions, Bayesian Lasso, Bayesian bridge regression, and a copula model of neuronal synchrony. The results show that this construction can provide an efficient framework for several kinds of constrained target distributions.
icml-2014-spherical-hamiltonian-monte-ca.tldr: Mapping constrained parameters onto a sphere lets Hamiltonian Monte Carlo handle boundaries implicitly and efficiently in the reported examples.

paragraphs: This paper studies regularized stochastic convex optimization with linear equality constraints. The objective combines learning under randomness with restrictions that the solution must satisfy. Earlier stochastic alternating direction method of multipliers algorithms addressed this class of problems, but their analyses produced convergence rates that were suboptimal.

The authors introduce two new stochastic ADMM methods with different guarantees. The first achieves an O(1/k) convergence rate for nonsmooth, strongly convex stochastic problems, where k denotes the iteration count. The paper identifies this rate as minimax optimal for that setting, giving a precise theoretical improvement under the stated objective assumptions.

The second method obtains an O(1/k²) rate for the smooth component of the problem. That component-specific result is progress toward an optimal rate; it does not assert the same rate for the entire stochastic constrained objective. Experiments indicate improved performance over competing ADMM methods. Together, the contributions strengthen convergence theory and provide empirical support for the proposed algorithms while distinguishing the conditions and scope of their two rate guarantees.
icml-2014-towards-an-optimal-stochastic-.tldr: Two stochastic ADMM methods improve convergence guarantees, including an optimal O(1/k) rate for nonsmooth strongly convex stochastic problems.

paragraphs: TD(lambda) is appealing because it combines inexpensive incremental updates with an intuitive forward view of learning. However, conventional TD(lambda) exactly matches that view only when updates are delayed until the end of an episode. With updates at every step, the correspondence is approximate because the conventional forward view assumes estimates remain fixed during the episode.

This paper introduces a forward view that explicitly allows estimates to change as learning proceeds. It then derives a TD(lambda) variant that matches the new view exactly. The algorithm uses a new eligibility trace, related to but distinct from the conventional accumulating and replacing traces that organize the updates.

The resulting method has the same overall computational complexity as TD(lambda), including when function approximation is used. In the reported empirical comparisons, it outperforms all tested TD(lambda) variations. The contribution links a more faithful account of online learning to an implementable algorithm, with exact forward-view correspondence and experimental evidence of improved performance at the same computational complexity.
icml-2014-true-online-td-lambda-8ae06319.tldr: True online TD(lambda) exactly matches a forward view that allows changing estimates while retaining conventional TD(lambda)'s computational complexity.

paragraphs: This paper studies bandit problems whose expected rewards have a unimodal structure over related choices. In the discrete case, the choices are vertices of a finite graph representing reward similarity. The authors derive asymptotic lower bounds on regret and introduce OSUB, an algorithm that matches those bounds.

OSUB's asymptotic regret does not depend on the total number of arms, showing how effectively it can exploit the specified structure. The paper also provides an upper bound for environments where expected rewards change smoothly over time. Numerical experiments support the analysis and report substantially better performance than the state-of-the-art algorithms considered.

For choices drawn from a bounded continuous interval, the authors briefly examine a different construction: discretize the interval appropriately and apply UCB. They show that this combination achieves order-optimal regret and empirically outperforms recently proposed methods designed for unimodal rewards. The results distinguish exact asymptotic matching in the discrete setting from order optimality in the continuous setting, while showing the value of using unimodal structure.
icml-2014-unimodal-bandits-regret-lower-.tldr: OSUB matches asymptotic regret lower bounds for discrete unimodal bandits, with regret independent of the total number of arms.
